item.title: Paraguay President Santiago Pena resigns following bank collapse
item.description: Paraguay's President Santiago Pena resigned after regulators seized Ueno Bank over risky lending, triggering protests, depositor panic and an impeachment debate.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Paraguay President Santiago Pena resigns following bank collapse

Paraguay President Santiago Pena resigns following bank collapse Paraguay's President Santiago Pena resigned after regulators seized Ueno Bank over risky lending, triggering protests, depositor panic and an impeachment debate.

Paraguayan President Santiago Pena | Image: Reuters

Press Trust of India 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 12:31 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned Thursday, days after the nation's central bank seized Ueno Bank, a major digital lender with close ties to his government.   Pena announced his resignation in a video posted to X, saying he was stepping down to preserve the country's stability and democratic institutions as massive protests rocked the capital, Asuncion, for a third day and lawmakers debated the president's impeachment.   "I have made the decision to submit my resignation as president of the republic," said Pena, a one-time investor in a company related to Ueno Bank. "I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

Pena offered an apology but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis.   "I also want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me." Also Read

He said his priority was ensuring depositors recovered their savings.   "Behind every deposit are years of hard work, sacrifice and family dreams," he said.   Ueno Bank, a major digital lender, went from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers.   The political upheaval and promises of relief leave a bigger question unanswered: how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno's holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

For many Paraguayans, the answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Pena's long-ruling Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.   "Santiago Pena and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."   Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Pena. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.   As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.   Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Colour, a leading Paraguayan newspaper.

Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.   Pena repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.   But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left.   Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fuelling public panic.   Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.

"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Pena's request.   Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud.   Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.   Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vazquez, the bank's parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank.

A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asuncion, the capital.   "We want your head, Pena!" they shouted. Their signs demanded Pena's impeachment, called him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded "Give us back our money."   Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.   Many demonstrators saw Ueno's collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.   "This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labour," said protester Belarmino Balbuena.

At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.

item.title: RBI proposes ₹100 crore limit on bank loans for agri infrastructure
item.description: The RBI has proposed a ₹100 crore aggregate loan limit per borrower for agricultural infrastructure under revised priority sector lending norms.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Banking / RBI proposes ₹100 crore limit on bank loans for agri infrastructure

RBI proposes ₹100 crore limit on bank loans for agri infrastructure The RBI has proposed a ₹100 crore aggregate loan limit per borrower for agricultural infrastructure under revised priority sector lending norms.

The Reserve Bank of India has proposed revised priority sector lending norms, including a ₹100 crore aggregate loan limit per borrower for agricultural infrastructure and higher eligibility limits for education and renewable energy loans. (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India Mumbai 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:16 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The Reserve Bank on Thursday proposed that loans for agricultural infrastructure will be subject to an aggregate sanctioned limit of Rs 100 crore per borrower from the banking system. As part of the ongoing effort towards consolidation of various instructions, the Reserve Bank of India said it has undertaken a review of the extant guidelines relating to Priority Sector Lending (PSL) and proposes to issue directions on the subject for different regulated entities, including commercial banks and regional rural banks. A draft direction on commercial banks proposed an aggregate loan limit of Rs 4 crore per borrowing entity for crop loans, medium and long-term loans for agriculture and allied activities, as well as loans for pre- and post-harvest activities.   It also said: "Loans for agriculture infrastructure will be subject to an aggregate sanctioned limit of Rs 100 crore per borrower from the banking system."   The lending to the agriculture sector will include farm credit (agriculture and allied activities), lending for agriculture infrastructure and ancillary activities. The draft further said that loans to individuals for educational purposes, including vocational courses, not exceeding Rs 25 lakh, will be considered as eligible for priority sector classification. Also Read

RBI tightens cyber oversight of non-bank payment system operators

Regarding renewable energy, it said bank loans up to a limit of Rs 35 crore to borrowers for renewable energy-based power generators and for renewable energy-based public utilities -- street lighting systems, remote village electrification -- will be eligible for priority sector classification. For individual households, the loan limit will be Rs 10 lakh per borrower, the draft said. Agriculture, MSMEs, exports, education, housing, social infrastructure, and renewable energy are among the categories under the priority sector. The RBI has also issued separate draft directions for small finance banks, local area banks, and regional rural banks. RBI has invited comments and feedback on the drafts by November 26.

item.title: Bangladesh garment factories close as workers clash with police in protests
item.description: Police in Bangladesh fired tear gas and used stun grenades Wednesday to disperse garment workers protesting for higher wages, police and witnesses said.
item.dc:creator: AP
item.content:encoded: Police in Bangladesh fired tear gas and used stun grenades Wednesday to disperse garment workers protesting for higher wages, police and witnesses said.Hundreds of factories remained shut after days of protests disrupted the country's garment industry, which earns about $40 billion a year from exports. Bangladesh has some 2,500 garment factories.Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 takas ($245), up from 12,500 takas. They say rising living costs and inflation have eroded their purchasing power.The industry employs about 4 million workers, mostly women from rural Bangladesh.After days of demonstrations in the capital, Dhaka, violence was reported in several industrial areas on its outskirts.In Fatullah, in Narayanganj district outside Dhaka, dozens of people were injured in clashes between protesters and police, according to media reports. Police fired tear gas and used stun grenades.Prothom Alo, Bangladesh's largest Bengali-language daily, reported that police arrested several protesters in Fatullah.About 100 factories remain shut in Ashulia, in Savar near Dhaka, said Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police.Workers also blocked a major highway in Gazipur district, another major industrial hub.More than 10,000 police officers had been deployed in Dhaka's Mirpur area, an epicenter of recent protests, to maintain order, said Mahidul Islam, a joint police commissioner.The government has responded to the wage demands by forming a new wage board.The board's chairman, Syed Azad Subhani, said workers would receive their first salaries under the new pay scale in January.

Home / Industry / News / Coal gasification can save ₹1.5 trillion in forex in 5-7 years: Coal secy

Coal gasification can save ₹1.5 trillion in forex in 5-7 years: Coal secy The Centre has committed financial incentives of ₹46,000 crore under two schemes to encourage coal gasification projects, said Coal Ministry Secretary Vikram Dev Dutt

Coal gasification projects require substantial upfront capital investment as well as support at the state level in terms of electricity, water supply and taxation | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India Panaji 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 2:26 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Coal gasification projects have the potential to save India around ₹1.5 trillion in foreign exchange over the next five to seven years through import substitution, Coal Ministry Secretary Vikram Dev Dutt said on Thursday. The Centre has committed financial incentives of ₹46,000 crore under two schemes to encourage coal gasification projects, Dutt said, addressing the 4th Conference of Mining Ministers on Reforms in the Mines and Coal Sector in South Goa. "Mining with a conscience" should be the guiding principle for responsible miners, the official added. He said coal gasification, which converts coal into synthetic gas (syngas), can help manufacture several products that India currently imports in substantial quantities.   "If the coal gasification projects get underway and gain scale, we would be succeeding in about five to seven years in saving about Rs one and a half trillion potentially of foreign exchange through this import substitution," Dutt said. Also Read

Coal imports by imported fuel-based power plants increase marginally in Aug

"Coal gasification has the potential of becoming an instrument of industrial diversification and regional development," the official said, urging coal-producing states to introduce supportive policies to attract investments in the sector. Methanol, ethanol, and ammonium nitrate used in explosives and inputs for direct reduced iron (DRI)-based steel production could be manufactured through coal gasification, he noted. Odisha and Maharashtra have already introduced incentive policies to promote coal gasification, with projects coming up in clusters in Odisha's Angul district and Maharashtra's Chandrapur belt, Dutt pointed out. He also called upon coal-rich states such as Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha to formulate policies offering incentives to investors, saying this would help attract projects and ensure that the benefits of central government schemes reach resource-rich regions. Coal gasification projects require substantial upfront capital investment as well as support at the state level in terms of electricity, water supply and taxation. Maharashtra and Odisha have taken steps in this direction, he said. Emphasising the employment potential of the sector, Dutt said gasification plants would generate jobs in downstream industries and benefit skilled and semi-skilled workers, besides strengthening local supply chains and creating additional economic activity. On coal sector reforms, Dutt said the commercial mining policy introduced in 2020 removed restrictions on end-use and sale of coal, paving the way for greater private participation. He said 137 mines had been allocated through 15 rounds of auctions, with captive and commercial mines accounting for around 20 per cent of India's total coal production. The government has also expanded the number of agencies authorised to undertake mineral exploration from 13 government agencies to 57, including 44 accredited private agencies, he informed. Dutt urged state governments to expedite land acquisition, public hearings, statutory clearances and other permissions required for operationalising coal blocks, saying delays in these processes often hinder mining projects. Faster operationalisation of auctioned coal blocks would ensure that states receive royalty and other revenue streams earlier, enabling them to fund development programmes, he stressed. Highlighting environmental initiatives, Dutt said the Coal Ministry had identified 147 mines for scientific closure over three years, of which 43 had already been scientifically closed. Scientific mine closure was not merely about technically sealing mines but also restoring degraded environments and repurposing mining areas after assessing the needs of local communities, he noted. The ministry has developed a digital tool called 'SuVikalp' to facilitate the assessment and repurposing of closed mines, he added. Dutt also stressed that the future of the coal sector should go beyond production targets and focus on productivity, technological advancement, transparency and environmental responsibility. "Mining with a conscience" should be the guiding principle for responsible miners, he said. The official also called for greater coordination between the Centre, state governments, coal companies and other stakeholders to make the sector competitive, efficient and environmentally sustainable. Union Minister for Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy, MoS for Mines Satish Chandra Dubey and Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant were present on the occasion.
